title: France’s riots and mounting debt reveal a country in disarray ahead of pivotal presidential election
gist: Chatham House says France's weekend of riots, debt near 119% of GDP and a bond sell-off six months before the 2027 presidential election expose a weakening European social contract that benefits Le Pen, Mélenchon and Germany's AfD.

insights.claim: France's public debt is approaching 119% of GDP, its deficit is the fourth highest in the eurozone, and it has been under an EU excessive deficit procedure since 2024.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: French sovereign risk is structurally elevated and sensitive to political shocks.
insights.locator: Its public debt is approaching 119 per cent of GDP

insights.claim: Images of the riots triggered a bond sell-off that added pressure on French debt, while riot damage projected above €1.2B and a 2027 riot-insurance scheme that could raise small-shopkeeper premiums sharpen fiscal and political strain.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Social unrest transmits directly into French spreads; watch OAT-Bund spread around further protests.

insights.claim: The parliamentary stalemate that followed Macron's 2024 dissolution of the National Assembly makes restoring financial discipline almost impossible.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Without a governing majority, deficit reduction is unlikely before the 2027 election.

insights.claim: A student-led protest over teaching conditions widened to unions and ex-'yellow vests' over living costs, drawing some 550,000 people by 17 October per the interior ministry (800,000 per organizers) before rioting, looting and a curfew in sensitive districts.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Mobilization is among the largest since the 2023 pension protests, raising the risk of further escalation.

insights.claim: Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon are both exploiting the unrest and remain the poll favourites to reach the second round of the 2027 presidential election.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Polarized second-round outcomes raise EU-budget and fiscal-policy risk premia for France.
insights.locator: France’s political centre no longer holds

insights.claim: Le Pen has said she would not fear a confrontation with Brussels over the EU budget if elected, and the AfD wants an end to Ukraine support and normalized Russian gas trade, so fragmentation in Paris and Berlin would weaken European defence and competitiveness.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A populist presidency in France would test EU fiscal rules and Ukraine support.
insights.locator: Le Pen has confirmed that she wouldn’t fear a confrontation

insights.claim: The AfD, which won 20.8% in the 2025 federal election, now polls at roughly 28–30%, driven by industrial-model erosion from energy costs, restricted export markets and Chinese competition.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: German political risk is rising as the industrial model deteriorates.

insights.claim: Europe's postwar bargain of rising prosperity and a better life for children has weakened just as AI threatens professions young people trained for, fuelling social demotion and political anger toward established parties.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: AI-driven job anxiety is an underpriced political driver of populist support.

insights.claim: Gabriel Attal proposed allowing temporary social-media restrictions during riots, and Italy's defence minister called the Milan riots a 'hybrid war against the West' via TikTok and social media, though no evidence of foreign interference has been established.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Governments are moving toward platform controls and hybrid-war framing of unrest.
insights.locator: former prime minister and presidential candidate Gabriel Attal’s proposal
